(Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.121.6">Psa 121:6</reference>).<div eID="gen10191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10192" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so that I forget--</hi>or, "have forgotten," that is, in my distress (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.18">Psa 107:18</reference>), and hence strength fails. <div eID="gen10192" type="x-p"/>
entries.7120b9428292e159b340c6a17e83c8f3f8a8d909: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6656"/><div sID="gen10193" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6656"/><hi type="bold">5. voice ... groaning--</hi>effect put for cause, my agony emaciates me. <div eID="gen10193" type="x-p"/>
entries.061642d436fe6d4f20d056205c72477218ebe395: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6657"/><div sID="gen10194" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6657"/>6-7. The figures express extreme loneliness. <div eID="gen10194" type="x-p"/>
entries.736d6cd631351f90b04748e3ade24bb367cd99a3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6658"/><div sID="gen10195" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6658"/><hi type="bold">8. sworn against me--</hi>or literally, "by me," wishing others as miserable as I am (<reference osisRef="Num.5.21">Nu 5:21</reference>). <div eID="gen10195" type="x-p"/>
entries.09c6856bdc14e57ce59240df15e38f89bfe33407: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6659"/><div sID="gen10196" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6659"/><hi type="bold">9. ashes--</hi>a figure of grief, my bread; weeping or tears, my drink (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.5">Psa 80:5</reference>). <div eID="gen10196" type="x-p"/>
entries.480a45ff56fdf8707482be9918f8554cc7be679b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6660"/><div sID="gen10197" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6660"/><hi type="bold">10. lifted ... cast me down--</hi>or, "cast me away" as stubble by a whirlwind (<reference osisRef="Isa.64.6">Is 64:6</reference>). <div eID="gen10197" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc9f998c6cc10dddc53083082196a71dd901c5e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6661"/><div sID="gen10198" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6661"/><hi type="bold">11. shadow ... declineth--</hi>soon to vanish in the darkness of night. <div eID="gen10198" type="x-p"/>
entries.40f6ae39ef5275f84431614ba36cacf2c7acc173: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6662"/><div sID="gen10199" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6662"/>12. Contrast with man's frailty (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.90.1-Ps.90.7">Psa 90:1-7</reference>).<div eID="gen10199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10200" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy remembrance--</hi>that by which Thou art remembered, Thy promise. <div eID="gen10200" type="x-p"/>
entries.cb6261dfccddfad4390afda147f32a4d40b1534f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6663"/><div sID="gen10201" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6663"/>13-14. Hence it is here adduced.<div eID="gen10201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10202" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for--</hi>or, "when."<div eID="gen10202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10203" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the set time, &c.--</hi>the time promised, the indication of which is the interest felt for Zion by the people of God. <div eID="gen10203" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b6271901176d0282511e3ab7986914cc17daef0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6664"/><div sID="gen10204" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6664"/>15-17. God's favor to the Church will affect her persecutors with fear. <div eID="gen10204" type="x-p"/>
entries.be0d382732df7139ac67718c8ef2bbd8dab26640: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6666"/><div sID="gen10206" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6666"/><hi type="bold">18. people ... created--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Ps.22.31">Psa 22:31</reference>), an organized body, as a Church. <div eID="gen10206" type="x-p"/>
entries.1c17b891b10cfb43684f9b29cd129efb37975652: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6667"/><div sID="gen10207" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6667"/><hi type="bold">19-22. For--</hi>or, "That," as introducing the statement of God's condescension. A summary of what shall be written.<div eID="gen10207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10208" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to loose ... appointed--</hi>or, "deliver" them (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.11">Psa 79:11</reference>). <div eID="gen10208" type="x-p"/>
entries.18a7928420974e957ca3d92fa383277aabfe81d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6669"/><div sID="gen10210" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6669"/>23-28. The writer, speaking for the Church, finds encouragement in the midst of all his distresses. God's eternal existence is a pledge of faithfulness to His promises.<div eID="gen10210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10211" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the way--</hi>of providence.<div eID="gen10211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10212" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">weakened--</hi>literally, "afflicted," and made fearful of a premature end, a figure of the apprehensions of the Church, lest God might not perform His promise, drawn from those of a person in view of the dangers of early death (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.89.47">Psa 89:47</reference>). Paul (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.10">He 1:10</reference>) quotes <reference osisRef="Ps.102.26-Ps.102.28">Psa 102:26-28</reference> as addressed to Christ in His divine nature. The scope of the Psalm, as already seen, so far from opposing, favors this view, especially by the sentiments of <reference osisRef="Ps.102.12-Ps.102.15">Psa 102:12-15</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.60.1">Is 60:1</reference>). The association of the Messiah with a day of future glory to the Church was very intimate in the minds of Old Testament writers; and with correct views of His nature it is very consistent that He should be addressed as the Lord and Head of His Church, who would bring about that glorious future on which they ever dwelt with fond delightful anticipations. <chapter eID="Ps.102"/>

entries.3bc982327ad08d24d76b220226c7ae7faf1d1440: <div eID="gen21974" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21975" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21976" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21976" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21975" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21977" type="x-p"/> The complaint and miserable state of the poor captives, <reference osisRef="Psa.102.1-Psa.102.11">Psa 102:1-11</reference>; the expectation of deliverance, <reference osisRef="Psa.102.12-Psa.102.14">Psa 102:12-14</reference>; the conversion of the heathen, <reference osisRef="Psa.102.15-Psa.102.18">Psa 102:15-18</reference>; the termination of the captivity, <reference osisRef="Psa.102.19-Psa.102.22">Psa 102:19-22</reference>; the great frailty of man, <reference osisRef="Psa.102.23">Psa 102:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.102.24">Psa 102:24</reference>; the unchangeableness of God, <reference osisRef="Psa.102.25-Psa.102.27">Psa 102:25-27</reference>; the permanence of the Church, <reference osisRef="Psa.102.28">Psa 102:28</reference>. <div eID="gen21977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21978" type="x-p"/> The Hebrew, and nearly all the Versions, give the following title to this Psalm: A prayer of the afflicted, when he is overwhelmed, and pours out his sighing before the Lord. There seems to be little doubt that this is the prayer of the captives in Babylon, when, towards the end of the captivity, they were almost worn out with oppression, cruelty, and distress. The Psalm has been attributed to Daniel, to Jeremiah, to Nehemiah, or to some of the other prophets who flourished during the time of the captivity. The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews has applied the twenty-fifth, twenty sixth, and twenty seventh verses to our Lord, and the perpetuity of his kingdom. <div eID="gen21978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21979" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21980" type="x-p"/> Hear my prayer - The chief parts of the Psalm answer well to the title: it is the language of the deepest distress, and well directed to Him from whom alone help can come.
entries.b62bda3583eb03971516c601f23f13e6a85c1941: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21981" type="x-p"/> My days are consumed like smoke - He represents himself (for the psalmist speaks in the name of the people) under the notion of a pile of combustible matter, placed upon a fire, which soon consumes it; part flying away in smoke, and the residue lying on the hearth in the form of charred coal and ashes. The Chaldeans were the fire, and the captive Jews the fuel, thus converted into smoke and ashes.
entries.1159a222959b96c5d339db9061f4e912532ac005: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen21981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21982" type="x-p"/> My heart is smitten, and withered like grass - The metaphor here is taken from grass cut down in the meadow. It is first smitten with the scythe, and then withered by the sun. Thus the Jews were smitten with the judgments of God; and they are now withered under the fire of the Chaldeans.
entries.dda598c43773b5ec39476a140c10ff1a0f2f68ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen21982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21983" type="x-p"/> I am like a pelican of the wilderness - It may be the pelican or the bittern. The original, קאת kaath, is mentioned <reference osisRef="Lev.11.18">Lev 11:18</reference> (note), and is there described. See the note. <div eID="gen21983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21984" type="x-p"/> Owl of the desert - כוש cos, some species of owl; probably the night raven. See the notes referred to above.
entries.6c7486ff0528fe1e64e637dcb98903976eb66e96: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen21984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21985" type="x-p"/> As a sparrow alone - צפור tsippor, seems to be often used for any small bird, such as the swallow, sparrow, or the like. Bochart supposes the screech owl is intended.
entries.d6d45c5a8bc15445e0e9f152ed46c59a54d48542: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen21985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21986" type="x-p"/> They that are mad against me are sworn against me - The Chaldeans are determined to destroy us; and they have bound themselves by oath to do it. See a similar case related <reference osisRef="Act.23.12-Act.23.14">Act 23:12-14</reference>, where a number of Jews had bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they had slain Paul.
entries.e785fcc7f3ff3f241a3eaad0af5918345e45d7a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen21986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21987" type="x-p"/> I have eaten ashes like bread - Fearful of what they might do, we all humbled ourselves before thee, and sought thy protection; well knowing that, unless we were supernaturally assisted, we must all have perished; our enemies having sworn our destruction.
entries.3e8979d5e9fa3ec825fbfc797059181029fa15f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen21987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21988" type="x-p"/> For thou hast lifted me up, and cast me down - Thou hast lifted me on high, that thou mightest dash me down with the greater force. <div eID="gen21988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21989" type="x-p"/> We were exalted in thy favor beyond any people, and now thou hast made us the lowest and most abject of the children of men.
entries.d9369c9161421e6d7e47fdea9eb9a77bd425f8a2: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen21989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21990" type="x-p"/> My days are like a shadow that declineth - Or rather, My days decline like the shadow. I have passed my meridian, and the sun of my prosperity is about to set for ever. There may be here an allusion to the declination of the sun towards the south, which, by shortening their days, would greatly lengthen their nights. Similar to the exclamation of a contemporary prophet, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.20">Jer 8:20</reference> : "The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved." There is now scarcely any human hope of our deliverance.
entries.902e0f318c1215c73771c79640f1581f47cef0de: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen21990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21991" type="x-p"/> But thou, O Lord, shalt endure for ever - Our life is a shadow; we can scarcely be called beings when compared with thee, for thou art eternal. Have mercy upon us, creatures of a day, and thy kindness shall be a memorial in all our generations.
entries.d9864cd48e625e337eb89988cf54f1b08a3af3af: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen21991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21992" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt arise, and have mercy upon Zion - While he is humbled at the footstool of mercy, and earnestly praying for mercy, an answer of peace is given; he is assured, not only that they shall be delivered, but that the time of deliverance is at hand. The set time - the seventy years predicted by Jeremiah, was ended; and God gave him to see that he was ever mindful of his promises.
entries.4a7381f136ca8994b55d5340d8e8bf9b02b6fa02: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen21992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21993" type="x-p"/> Thy servants take pleasure in her stones - Though Jerusalem was at this time in a heap of ruins, yet even her rubbish was sacred in the eyes of the pious; for this had been the city of the great King.
entries.5652323dd176a22350a2d14ff18d3b673a60ca5e: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen21993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21994" type="x-p"/> So the heathen shall fear the name of the Lord - It is granted that after the edict of Cyrus to restore and rebuild Jerusalem which was about four hundred and ninety years before Christ, the name of the true God was more generally known among the heathen; and the translating the Sacred Writings into Greek, by the command of Ptolemy Philadelphus, king of Egypt, about two hundred and eighty-five years before the Christian era, spread a measure of the light of God in the Gentile world which they had not before seen. Add to this the disperson of the Jews into different parts of the Roman empire, after Judea became a Roman province, which took place about sixty years before the advent of our Lord; and we may consider these as so many preparatory steps to the conversion of the heathen by the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ. And to this last general illumination of the Gentile world the psalmist must allude here, when he speaks of "the heathen fearing God's name, and all the kings of the earth his glory."
entries.13d7d9fba692a682ef5968c3873a20dde6c64459: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen21994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21995" type="x-p"/> When the Lord shall build up Zion - It is such a difficult thing, so wholly improbable, so far out of the reach of human power, that when God does it, he must manifest his power and glory in a most extraordinary manner.
entries.30836ca129698d40b86b4d386560e75215cd64c6: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen21995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21996" type="x-p"/> The prayer of the destitute - הערער haarar of him who is laid in utter ruin, who is entirely wasted.
entries.94f9a7a03f2709e74acaa9379e0668a18e36c15f: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen21996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21997" type="x-p"/> The people which shall be created - "The Gentiles, who shall be brought to the knowledge of salvation by Christ," as the Syriac states in its inscription to this Psalm: how often the conversion of the soul to God is represented as a new creation, no reader of the New Testament need be told. See <reference osisRef="Eph.2.10">Eph 2:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.24">Eph 4:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.17">2Cor 5:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.6.15">Gal 6:15</reference>. Even the publication of the Gospel, and its influence among men, is represented under the notion of "creating a new heaven and a new earth," <reference osisRef="Isa.65.17">Isa 65:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.18">Isa 65:18</reference>.
entries.02cd2571548f32020acfbf1409744ca57e8f2c22: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen21997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21998" type="x-p"/> For he hath looked down - This, with the three following verses, seems to me to contain a glorious prophecy of the incarnation of Christ, and the gathering in of the Jews and the Gentiles to him. The Lord looks down from heaven, and sees the whole earth groaning and travailing in pain; his eye affects his heart, and he purposes their salvation.
entries.eabd5bf7af3ded39c7b1f7ccb7cf6d5c0d323786: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen21998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21999" type="x-p"/> To hear the groaning - By sin, all the inhabitants of the earth are miserable. They have broken the Divine laws, are under the arrest of judgment, and all cast into prison, They have been tried, found guilty, and appointed to die; they groan under their chains, are alarmed at the prospect of death, and implore mercy.
entries.a50798c7cd2eebda1969083e755b1946a4f14043: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen21999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22000" type="x-p"/> To declare the name of the Lord - To publish that Messenger of the Covenant in whom the name of the Lord is, that Messiah in whom the fullness of the Godhead dwelt; and to commence at Jerusalem, that the first offers of mercy might be made to the Jews, from whom the word of reconciliation was to go out to all the ends of the earth.
entries.2472ab6d0e99a9f67991dfdaeebc20ff2514c967: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen22000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22001" type="x-p"/> When the people are gathered together - When all the Gentiles are enlightened, and the kings of the earth brought to pay homage to the King of kings.
entries.4fa89c232e96468b83876f4a71baa995668e1e92: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen22001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22002" type="x-p"/> He weakened my strength in the way - We are brought so low in our captivity by oppression, by every species of hard usage, and by death, that there is now no hope of our restoration by any efforts of our own.
entries.7a0acf12da1cab295237e300df3dc13f16cc01c6: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen22002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22003" type="x-p"/> I said, O my God - This and the following verses seem to be the form of prayer which the captives used previously to their deliverance. <div eID="gen22003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22004" type="x-p"/> Thy years are throughout all generations - This was a frequent argument used to induce God to hear prayer. We are frail and perishing; thou art everlasting: deliver us, and we will glorify thee.
entries.d7e682faac1f462949805f60672a941dec870bf4: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen22004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22005" type="x-p"/> Of old hast thou laid the foundation - None taught of God ever imagined the world to have been eternal. Of old, לפנים lephanim, before there were any faces or appearances, thou didst lay the foundations of the earth. It was created by thee; it did not grow by accretion or aggregation from a pre-existent nucleus. There was nothing; and thou didst produce being - substance or matter. Out of that created matter thou didst make the earth and the heavens.
entries.a57d1235934f64ff3f920b17649f9c02e4f80562: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen22005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22006" type="x-p"/> They shall perish - Nothing can be eternal a parte ante, or a parte post, but thyself. Even that which thou hast created, because not necessarily eternal, must be perishable; necessary duration belongs to God only; and it is by his will and energy alone that universal nature is preserved in existence, and preserved from running into speedy disorder, decay, and ruin. <div eID="gen22006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22007" type="x-p"/> Yea, all of them shall wax old - Every thing must deteriorate, unless preserved by thy renewing and invigorating energy. Even the heavens and the earth are subject to this law; for that which is not, from the infinite perfection of its own nature, Eternal, must be perishable; therefore the heavens and the earth must necessarily come to an end. They contain the seeds of their own dissolution. It is true that in sublunary things, the vicissitudes of seasons is a sort of check to the principle of dissolution; but it only partially corrects this tendency. Even the productions of the earth wear out or deteriorate. Plant the same seed or grain for several years consecutively, and it degenerates so as at last not to be worth the labor of tillage, however expensively the soil may be manured in which it is planted. I may instance in wheat and in the potatoe, the two grand supporters of life in European countries. All other seeds and plants, as far as they have fallen under my observation, are subject to the same law.
entries.5b835ac2a10510eb51bdb5431dbd86eac02c3047: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen22007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22008" type="x-p"/> But thou art the same - ואתה הוא veattah Hu, but thou art He, that is, The Eternal; and, consequently, he who only has immortality. <div eID="gen22008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22009" type="x-p"/> Thy years shall have no end - לא יתמו lo yittammu, "they shall not be completed." Every thing has its revolution - its conception, growth, perfection, decay, dissolution, and death, or corruption. It may be said that regeneration restores all these substances; and so it does in a measure, but not without deterioration. The breed of animals, as well as vegetables, wears out; but God's eternal round has no completion. I repeat it, - what is necessarily eternal is unchangeable and imperishable; all created beings are perishable and mutable, because not eternal. God alone is eternal; therefore God alone is imperishable and immutable.
entries.4a1b72998f59e77f63fef98b9297ba8082b60aee: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen22009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22010" type="x-p"/> The children of thy servants shall continue - Thy Church shall be permanent, because founded on thee, it shall live throughout all the revolutions of time. And as thy followers are made partakers of the Divine nature they shall live in union with God in the other world, deriving eternal duration from the inexhaustible Fountain of being. Nothing can be permanent but by God's supporting and renewing influence.  <chapter eID="Ps.102"/> <div eID="gen22010" type="x-p"/>

entries.82b115f79ffba7f4ff4afb6b97f40ec1887c5f8e: <div eID="gen9979" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Prayer of a Patient Sufferer for Himself and for the Jerusalem That Lies in Ruins</title> <div sID="gen9980" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.101.1-Ps.101.8">Psa 101:1-8</reference> utters the sigh: <hi type="italic">When wilt Thou come to me?</hi> and Ps 102 with the inscription: <hi type="italic">Prayer for an afflicted one when he pineth away and poureth forth his complaint before Jahve</hi>, prays, <hi type="italic">Let my prayer come unto Thee</hi>. It is to be taken, too, just as personally as it sounds, and the person is not to be construed into a nation. The song of the עני is, however, certainly a national song; the poet is a servant of Jahve, who shares the calamity that has befallen Jerusalem and its homeless people, both in outward circumstances and in the very depth of his soul. עטף signifies to pine away, languish, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.61.3">Psa 61:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.16">Isa 57:16</reference>; and שׁפך שׂיחו to pour out one’s thoughts and complaints, one’s anxious care, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.142.3">Psa 142:3</reference>, cf. 1Sa 1:15. <div eID="gen9980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9981" type="x-p"/> As in the case already with many of the preceding Psalms, the deutero-Isaianic impression accompanies us in connection with this Psalm also, even to the end; and the further we get in it the more marked does the echo of its prophetical prototype become. The poet also allies himself with earlier Psalms, such as Ps 22, Ps 69, and <reference osisRef="Ps.79.1-Ps.79.13">Psa 79:1-13</reference>, although himself capable of lofty poetic flight, in return for which he makes us feel the absence of any safely progressive unfolding of the thoughts.
entries.3cfed1965cef1a10ff88f3d0adebdc5fab5ab2ce: <reference osisRef="Ps.102.1-Ps.102.2">Psa 102:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen9981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9982" type="x-p"/> The Psalm opens with familiar expressions of prayer, such as rise in the heart and mouth of the praying one without his feeling that they are of foreign origin; cf. more especially <reference osisRef="Ps.39.13">Psa 39:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.7">Psa 18:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.3">Psa 88:3</reference>; and on <reference osisRef="Ps.102.3">Psa 102:3</reference> : <reference osisRef="Ps.27.9">Psa 27:9</reference> (<hi type="italic">Hide not Thy face from me</hi>); <reference osisRef="Ps.59.17">Psa 59:17</reference> (ביום צר לי); <reference osisRef="Ps.31.3">Psa 31:3</reference> and frequently (<hi type="italic">Incline Thine ear unto me</hi>); <reference osisRef="Ps.56.10">Psa 56:10</reference> (ביום אקוא); <reference osisRef="Ps.69.8">Psa 69:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.143.7">Psa 143:7</reference> (מהר ענני).
entries.f809b09911cc72db43705c334f5263d3dfe16948: <reference osisRef="Ps.102.3-Ps.102.5">Psa 102:3-5</reference> <div eID="gen9982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9983" type="x-p"/> From this point onward the Psalm becomes original. Concerning the <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> in בעשׁן, vid., on Psa 37:20. The reading כּמו קד (in the Karaite Ben-Jerucham) enriches the lexicon in the same sense with a word which has scarcely had any existence. מוקד (Arabic <hi type="italic">mauḳid</hi>) signifies here, as in other instances, a hearth. נחרוּ is, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.69.4">Psa 69:4</reference>, <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi>: my bones are heated through with a fever-heat, as a hearth with the smouldering fire that is on it. הוּכּה (cf. יגודּוּ, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.21">Psa 94:21</reference>) is used exactly as in Hos 9:16, cf. Psa 121:5. The heart is said to dry up when the life’s blood, of which it is the reservoir, fails. The verb שׁכח is followed by מן of dislike. On the cleaving of the bones to the flesh from being baked, i.e., to the skin (Arabic <hi type="italic">bašar</hi>, in accordance with the radical signification, the surface of the body = the skin, from בשׂר, to brush along, rub, scrape, scratch on the surface), cf. <reference osisRef="Job.19.20">Job 19:20</reference>; Lam 4:8. ל (אל) with דּבק is used just like בּ. It is unnecessary, with Böttcher, to draw מקּול אנחתי to Psa 102:5. Continuous straining of the voice, especially in connection with persevering prayer arising from inward conflict, does really make the body waste away.
entries.74e5b5ebf6bab68e234e28df7514a3b339d98f55: <reference osisRef="Ps.102.6-Ps.102.8">Psa 102:6-8</reference> קאת (construct of קאת or קאת from קאה, vid., <hi type="italic">Isaiah</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Isa.34.11-Isa.34.12">Isa 34:11-12</reference>), according to the lxx, is the pelican, and כּוס is the night-raven or the little horned-owl.<note placement="foot">The lxx renders it: I am like a pelican of the desert, I am become as a night-raven upon a ruined place (οἰκοπέδῳ). In harmony with the lxx, Saadia (as also the Arabic version edited by Erpenius, the Samaritan Arabic, and Abulwalîd) renders קאת by Arab. <hi type="italic">qûq</hi> (here and in <reference osisRef="Lev.11.18">Lev 11:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.14.17">Deu 14:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.34.17">Isa 34:17</reference>), and כוס by Arab. <hi type="italic">bûm</hi>; the latter (<hi type="italic">bum</hi>) is an onomatopoetic name of the owl, and the former (<hi type="italic">k[uk[</hi>) does not even signify the owl or horned-owl (although the small horned-owl is called <hi type="italic">um kuéik</hi> in Egypt, and in Africa <hi type="italic">abu kuéik</hi>; vid., the dictionaries of Bocthor and Marcel s.v. <hi type="italic">chouette</hi>), but the pelican, the “long-necked water-bird” (Damiri after the lexicon <hi type="italic">el - ‛Obâb</hi> of Hasan ben-Mohammed el-Saghani). The Graeco-Veneta also renders קאת with πελεκάν, - the Peshito, however, with Syr. <hi type="italic">qāqā'</hi>. What Ephrem on <reference osisRef="Deut.14.17">Deu 14:17</reference> and the <hi type="italic">Physiologus Syrus</hi> (ed. <hi type="italic">Tychsen</hi>, p. 13, cf. pp. 110 f). say of Syr. <hi type="italic">qāqā'</hi>, viz., that it is a marsh-bird, is very fond of its young ones, dwells in desolate places, and is incessantly noisy, likewise points to the pelican, although the Syrian lexicographers vary. Cf. also Oedmann, <hi type="italic">Vermischte Sammlungen</hi>, Heft 3, Cap. 6. (Fleischer after a communication from Rodiger.)</note> דּמה obtains the signification to be like, equal (<hi type="italic">aequalem esse</hi>), from the radical signification to be flat, even, and to spread out flat (as the Dutch have already recognised). They are both unclean creatures, which are fond of the loneliness of the desert and ruined places. To such a wilderness, that of the exile, is the poet unwillingly transported. He passes the nights without sleep (שׁקד, to watch during the time for sleep), and is therefore like a bird sitting lonesome (בּודד, Syriac erroneously נודד) upon the roof whilst all in the house beneath are sleeping. The <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.102.8">Psa 102:8</reference> separates that which is come to be from the ground of the “becoming” and the “becoming” itself. His grief is that his enemies reproach him as one forsaken of God. מהולל, <hi type="italic">part. Poal</hi>, is one made or become mad, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.2">Ecc 2:2</reference> : my mad ones = those who are mad against me. These swear by him, inasmuch as they say when they want to curse: “God do unto thee as unto this man,” which is to be explained according to <reference osisRef="Isa.65.15">Isa 65:15</reference>; Jer 29:22.
entries.650ecbbaba149480e9a6290545cdd86bb8c2decc: <reference osisRef="Ps.102.9-Ps.102.11">Psa 102:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen9983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9984" type="x-p"/> Ashes are his bread (cf. <reference osisRef="Lam.3.16">Lam 3:16</reference>), inasmuch as he, a mourner, sits in ashes, and has thrown ashes all over himself, <reference osisRef="Job.2.8">Job 2:8</reference>; Eze 27:30. The infected שׁקּוי has שׁקּוּ = שׁקּוּו for its principal form, instead of which it is שׁקּוּי in Hos 2:7. “That Thou hast lifted me up and cast me down” is to be understood according to Job 30:22. First of all God has taken away the firm ground from under his feet, then from aloft He has cast him to the ground - an emblem of the lot of Israel, which is removed from its fatherland and cast into exile, i.e., into a strange land. In that passage the days of his life are כּצל נטוּי, like a lengthened shadow, which grows longer and longer until it is entirely lost in darkness, Psa 109:23. Another figure follows: he there becomes like an (uprooted) plant which dries up.
entries.059dc520ebef54fb148625b9e32ef905d2aba59e: <reference osisRef="Ps.102.12-Ps.102.14">Psa 102:12-14</reference> <div eID="gen9984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9985" type="x-p"/> When the church in its individual members dies off on a foreign soil, still its God, the unchangeable One, remains, and therein the promise has the guarantee of its fulfilment. Faith lays hold upon this guarantee as in Ps 90. It becomes clear from <reference osisRef="Ps.9.8">Psa 9:8</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lam.5.19">Lam 5:19</reference> how תּשׁב is to be understood. The Name which Jahve makes Himself by self-attestation never falls a prey to the dead past, it is His ever-living memorial (זכר, <reference osisRef="Exod.3.15">Exo 3:15</reference>). Thus, too, will He restore Jerusalem; the limit, or appointed time, to which the promise points is, as his longing tells the poet, now come. מועד, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.75.3">Psa 75:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.3">Hab 2:3</reference>, is the juncture, when the redemption by means of the judgment on the enemies of Israel shall dawn. לחננהּ, from the infinitive חנן, has <hi type="italic">ĕ</hi>, flattened from <hi type="italic">ă</hi>, in an entirely closed syllable. רצה <hi type="italic">seq. acc.</hi> signifies to have pleasure in anything, to cling to it with delight; and חנן, according to <reference osisRef="Prov.14.21">Pro 14:21</reference>, affirms a compassionate, tender love of the object. The servants of God do not feel at home in Babylon, but their loving yearning lingers over the ruins, the stones and the heaps of the rubbish (<reference osisRef="Neh.4.2">Neh 4:2</reference>), of Jerusalem.
entries.317851b70330cb14a8cf26f011c14392bfeae711: <reference osisRef="Ps.102.15-Ps.102.17">Psa 102:15-17</reference> <div eID="gen9985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9986" type="x-p"/> With וייראוּ we are told what will take place when that which is expected in <reference osisRef="Ps.102.14">Psa 102:14</reference> comes to pass, and at the same time the fulfilment of that which is longed for is thereby urged home upon God: Jahve’s own honour depends upon it, since the restoration of Jerusalem will become the means of the conversion of the world - a fundamental thought of <reference osisRef="Isa.40.1">Isa 40:1</reference> (cf. more particularly <reference osisRef="Isa.59.19">Isa 59:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.2">Isa 60:2</reference>), which is also called to mind in the expression of this strophe. This prophetic prospect (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.1-Isa.40.5">Isa 40:1-5</reference>) that the restoration of Jerusalem will take place simultaneously with the glorious parusia of Jahve re-echoes here in a lyric form. כּי, <reference osisRef="Ps.102.17">Psa 102:17</reference>, states the ground of the reverence, just as <reference osisRef="Ps.102.20">Psa 102:20</reference> the ground of the praise. The people of the Exile are called in <reference osisRef="Ps.102.18">Psa 102:18</reference> הערער, from ערר, to be naked: homeless, powerless, honourless, and in the eyes of men, prospectless. The lxx renders this word in <reference osisRef="Jer.17.6">Jer 17:6</reference> ἀγριομυρίκη, and its plural, formed by an internal change of vowel, ערוער, in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.6">Jer 48:6</reference> ὄνος ἄγριος, which are only particularizations of the primary notion of that which is stark naked, neglected, wild. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.102.18">Psa 102:18</reference> </hi>is an echo off Psa 22:25. In the mirror of this and of other Psalms written in times of affliction the Israel of the Exile saw itself reflected.
entries.d321b8a26a7c0a65704699e0b456b44b45984113: <reference osisRef="Ps.102.18-Ps.102.22">Psa 102:18-22</reference> <div eID="gen9986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9987" type="x-p"/> The poet goes on advancing motives to Jahve for the fulfilment of his desire, by holding up to Him what will take place when He shall have restored Zion. The evangel of God’s redemptive deed will be written down for succeeding generations, and a new, created people, i.e., a people coming into existence, the church of the future, shall praise God the Redeemer for it. דּור אחרון as in <reference osisRef="Ps.48.14">Psa 48:14</reference>; Psa 78:4. עם נברא like עם נולד Ps 22:32, perhaps with reference to deutero-Isaianic passages like Isa 43:17. On <reference osisRef="Ps.102.20">Psa 102:20</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.63.15">Isa 63:15</reference>; in <reference osisRef="Ps.102.21">Psa 102:21</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.42.7">Isa 42:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Isa 61:1</reference>) the deutero-Isaianic colouring is very evident. And <reference osisRef="Ps.102.21">Psa 102:21</reference> rests still more verbally upon Psa 79:11. The people of the Exile are as it were in prison and chains (אסיר), and are advancing towards their destruction (בּני תמוּתה), if God does not interpose. Those who have returned home are the subject to לספּר. בּ in <reference osisRef="Ps.102.23">Psa 102:23</reference> introduces that which takes place simultaneously: with the release of Israel from servitude is united the conversion of the world. נקבּץ occurs in the same connection as in Isa 60:4. After having thus revelled in the glory of the time of redemption the poet comes back to himself and gives form to his prayer on his own behalf.
entries.82ae2429e1fe70b97e1dc0d12792b2bc90bc75ec: <reference osisRef="Ps.102.23-Ps.102.28">Psa 102:23-28</reference> <div eID="gen9987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9988" type="x-p"/> On the way (ב as in <reference osisRef="Ps.110.7">Psa 110:7</reference>) - not “by means of the way” (ב as in <reference osisRef="Ps.105.18">Psa 105:18</reference>), in connection with which one would expect of find some attributive minuter definition of the way - God hath bowed down his strength (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.8.2">Deu 8:2</reference>); it was therefore a troublous, toilsome way which he has been led, together with his people. He has shortened his days, so that he only drags on wearily, and has only a short distance still before him before he is entirely overcome. The <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> כחו (lxx ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ) may be understood of God’s irresistible might, as in <reference osisRef="Job.23.6">Job 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.30.18">Job 30:18</reference>, but in connection with it the designation of the object is felt to be wanting. The introductory אמר (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.10.2">Job 10:2</reference>), which announces a definite moulding of the utterance, serves to give prominence to the petition that follows. In the expression אל־תּעלני life is conceived of as a line the length of which accords with nature; to die before one’s time is a being taken up out of this course, so that the second half of the line is not lived through (Ps 55:24, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.10">Isa 38:10</reference>). The prayer not to sweep him away before his time, the poet supports not by the eternity of God in itself, but by the work of the rejuvenation of the world and of the restoration of Israel that is to be looked for, which He can and will bring to an accomplishment, because He is the ever-living One. The longing to see this new time is the final ground of the poet’s prayer for the prolonging of his life. The confession of God the Creator in <reference osisRef="Ps.102.26">Psa 102:26</reference> reminds one in its form of <reference osisRef="Isa.48.13">Isa 48:13</reference>, cf. Psa 44:24. המּה in <reference osisRef="Ps.102.27">Psa 102:27</reference> refers to the two great divisions of the universe. The fact that God will create heaven and earth anew is a revelation that is indicated even in <reference osisRef="Isa.34.4">Isa 34:4</reference>, but is first of all expressed more fully and in many ways in the second part of the Book of Isaiah, viz., <reference osisRef="Isa.51.6">Isa 51:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.16">Isa 51:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.17">Isa 65:17</reference>; Isa 66:22. It is clear from the agreement in the figure of the garment (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.6">Isa 51:6</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.50.9">Psa 50:9</reference>) and in the expression (עמד, <hi type="italic">perstare</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.66.22">Isa 66:22</reference>) that the poet has gained this knowledge from the prophet. The expressive אתּה הוּא, Thou art He, i.e., unalterably the same One, is also taken from the mouth of the prophet, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.4">Isa 41:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.10">Isa 43:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.46.4">Isa 46:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.12">Isa 48:12</reference>; הוּא is a predicate, and denotes the identity (sameness) of Jahve (Hofmann, <hi type="italic">Schriftbeweis</hi>, i. 63). In v. 29 also, in which the prayer for a lengthening of life tapers off to a point, we hear <reference osisRef="Isa.65.2">Isa 65:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.22">Isa 66:22</reference> re-echoed. And from the fact that in the mind of the poet as of the prophet the post-exilic Jerusalem and the final new Jerusalem upon the new earth under a new heaven blend together, it is evident that not merely in the time of Hezekiah or of Manasseh (assuming that <reference osisRef="Isa.40.1">Isa 40:1</reference> are by the old Isaiah), but also even in the second half of the Exile, such a perspectively foreshortened view was possible. When, moreover, the writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews at once refers <reference osisRef="Ps.102.26-Ps.102.28">Psa 102:26-28</reference> to Christ, this is justified by the fact that the God whom the poet confesses as the unchangeable One is Jahve who is to come.  <chapter eID="Ps.102"/> <div eID="gen9988" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 102
This prayer seems to have been dictated to the faithful when they were languishing in captivity in Babylon. Sorrowful and humbled, they first bewail their afflictions. In the next place, they plead with God for the restoration of the holy city and temple. To encourage themselves to come before him in prayer with the greater confidence, they call to remembrance the Divine promises in reference to the happy renovation both of the kingdom and of the priesthood; and they not only assure themselves of deliverance from captivity, but also beseech God to bring kings and nations in subjection to himself. In the close of the psalm, after having interposed a brief complaint concerning their distressing and afflicted condition, they draw consolation from the eternity of God; for, in adopting his servants to a better hope, he has separated them from the common lot of men.
A prayer for the afflicted, when he shall be shut up, and shall pour out his meditation before Jehovah.
Whoever of the prophets composed this psalm, it is certain that he dictated it to the faithful as a form of prayer for the re-establishment of the temple and the city. Some limit it to the time when, after the return of the Jews from Babylon, the building of the temple was hindered by the neighboring nations; but with this I cannot agree. I am rather of opinion that the poem was written before the return of the people, when the time of their promised deliverance was just at hand; for then the prophets began to be more earnest in lifting up the hearts of the godly according to these words of Isaiah, (Isaiah 40:1) “Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God.”
“This plaintive poem was written by some pious exile towards the expiration of the seventy years of captivity during which the people of Israel were detained in Babylon. [...] The author of the psalm had most probably been carried away captive in early youth. He had survived nearly to the end of the term, and now, worn with cares and anxieties, he was earnest with God that deliverance might speedily arrive, lest he should sink into the grave without revisiting the delightful scenes by which his imagination was enraptured, without witnessing the fulfillment of the hopes which the prophets of God had excited by the predictions which they had delivered relative to the returning prosperity of his beloved country.” — Walford. Hammond thinks that the psalm was written by Nehemiah, after the return of Ezra with commission for rebuilding the temple. See Nehemiah 1:3, etc. Others ascribe it to Jeremiah or Daniel.
The design of the sacred poet was, not only to inspire the people with courage, but also to excite in them greater care about the welfare of the Church. The title of the psalm indicates the end and purpose which it was intended to serve. Those who translate the verbs in the past tense, A prayer for the afflicted, when he was in distress, and poured out his meditation,
“Sa plainte.” — Fr. “His complaint.”
seem to give an incorrect view of the mind of the prophet. He rather intended to relieve the sorrow of those whose hearts he saw depressed; as if he had said, Although you may be afflicted with anguish and despair, you must not on that account desist from prayer. Some translate the verb עטף, ataph, when he shall hide himself, and conceive that this is a metaphorical expression of the gesture of a man engaged in prayer, when, on account of his grief, unable to lift up his face, he, as it were, hides himself, and keeps his head wrapped up in his bosom. But there appears to me to be an elegant play upon the words, when the distresses of the mind, and its being shut up, are spoken of, on the one hand, and the pouring out of prayers on the other; teaching us that, when we are so shut up by grief as to shun the light and presence of men, the gate is so far from being shut against our prayers, that then in truth is the most proper season for engaging in prayer, for it is a singular alleviation of our sorrows when we have opportunity freely to pour out our hearts before God. The verb שוח, suach, often denotes to pray; but, as it also signifies to meditate, the noun derived from it properly means, in this place, meditation. It is, moreover, to be observed that, by these words, the Psalmist admonishes the Israelites as to the frame of mind with which it became them to use this form of prayer at the throne of grace; as if he had said, that he prescribed it to those only who were distressed on account of the desolate condition of the Church.
Psalm 102:1-2
1. O Jehovah! hear my prayer, and let my cry come to thee. 2. Hide not thy face from me in the day of my affliction; incline thy ear to me: in the day when I cry make haste, answer me.
 
1 O Jehovah! hear my prayer This earnestness shows, again, that these words were not dictated to be pronounced by the careless and light-hearted, which could not have been done without grossly insulting God. In speaking thus, the captive Jews bear testimony to the severe and excruciating distress which they endured, and to the ardent desire to obtain some alleviation with which they were inflamed. No person could utter these words with the mouth without profaning the name of God, unless he were, at the same time, actuated by a sincere and earnest affection of heart. We ought particularly to attend to the circumstance already adverted to, that we are thus stirred up by the Holy Spirit to the duty of prayer in behalf of the common welfare of the Church. Whilst each man takes sufficient care of his own individual interests, there is scarcely one in a hundred affected as he ought to be with the calamities of the Church. We have, therefore, the more need of incitements, even as we see the prophet here endeavoring, by an accumulation of words, to correct our coldness and sloth. I admit that the heart ought to move and direct the tongue to prayer; but, as it often flags or performs its duty in a slow and sluggish manner, it requires to be aided by the tongue. There is here a reciprocal influence. As the heart, on the one hand, ought to go before the words, and frame them, so the tongue, on the other, aids and remedies the coldness and torpor of the heart. True believers may indeed often pray not only earnestly but also fervently, while yet not a single word proceeds from the mouth. There is, however, no doubt that by crying the prophet means the vehemence into which grief constrains us to break forth.

                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> the chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren of death.</ns0:note> those that are appointed to death <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">To release his poor Captives out of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> and, which is more, from the Chains and Fetters of Sin and Satan, and from eternal destruction.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 To declare the name of the LORD in Zion, and his praise in Jerusalem <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">That they being delivered might publish and celebrate the name and praises of God in his Church.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 When the people are gathered together, and the kingdoms to praise the LORD <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">When the Gentiles shall gather themselves to the Jews, and join with them in the praise and worship of the true God, and of the Messias. This Verse seems to be added to inti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mate that although the Psalmist in this Psalm respects the de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liverance of the Jews out of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> yet he had a further de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sign and a principal respect unto that greater and more ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neral deliverance of his Church and People by the Messias.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 He <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">To wit, God, to whom he ascribes these Calamities, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 10. to whom therefore he addresseth himself for relief.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> afflict<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed.</ns0:note> weakned my strength in the way <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther 1. in the midst of our expectations. Whilest we are expecting the accomplishment of thy promise either of bring<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing us out of <ns0:hi>Babylon;</ns0:hi> or of sending the Messias, we faint and one of us perish after another, and our hope is like the giving up of the Ghost. Or rather 2. in the midst of the course of our lives. Which sence is confirmed, 1. from the following Clause. Which after the manner explains the for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mer, <ns0:hi>he shortned my days;</ns0:hi> as also from the next Verse where he begs relief from God against this misery in these words, <ns0:hi>take me not away in the midst of my days.</ns0:hi> 2. From the use of this word <ns0:hi>way,</ns0:hi> which is used for the course of a mans life, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 2. 12. and (which comes to the same thing) for the course of a journey as it is opposed to the end of the jour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ney, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 24. 27. <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 23. 20. and elsewhere; the life of man being oft compared to a journeying or travelling and death to his journeys end. And the Psalmist here speaks (as other sacred Writers do elsewhere, and as all sorts of Wri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ters frequently do) of the whole Commonwealth as of one man, and of its continuance as of the life of one man. And so this seems to be the matter of his complaint and humble expostulation with God, O Lord, thou didst chuse us out of all the World to be thy peculiar people, and didst plant us in <ns0:hi>Ganaan,</ns0:hi> and cause a glorious Temple to be built to thy name to be the onely place of thy publick and solemn wor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ship in the World, and didst make great and glorious pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mises, that thine <ns0:hi>eyes and heart</ns0:hi> should be <ns0:hi>upon it perpetually,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 9. 3. and that thy people should be planted in thy land so as not to be moved any more or afflicted, as they had been in the days of the Judges, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 7. 10, 11. From whence we promised to our selves a long and setled prospe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rity. But, alas, how soon were our hopes blasted, not long after the beginning of our settlement, in <ns0:hi>Rehoboams</ns0:hi> time, and so successively in the course of our affairs under the following Kings, till at last thou didst give us up to ruine and desola<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, as at this day. And this he doth not alledge to accuse God or excuse himself or his people, but onely that he might move the Divine Majesty to shew them some pity consider<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the shortness of their days, and his own Eternity, as he pursues the argument in the following Verses.</ns0:note>, he shortned my days <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The days of my life, or of my prosperous state, as above <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 11. for adversity is a kind of death, and is frequently so called.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 I said, O my God; <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 36. 20<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Heb.</ns0:note> take me not away <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Do not wholly cut off and destroy thy people of <ns0:hi>Israel.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> in the midst of my days <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Before they come to a full age and stature, and to the ple<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nary possession of thy promises, and especially of that great and fundamental promise of the Messiah in and by whom alone their happiness is to be compleated, and until whose coming thy Church is in its nonage; of which see <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4. 1, 2, 3, 4. Possibly the Psalmist (whom some learned Interpre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ters suppose to be <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi>) may have respect to that Prophecy, <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 9. 24, 25. which probably was published before this time: for this time was almost precisely the midst of the days between the building of the material Temple by <ns0:hi>Solomon,</ns0:hi> and the building of the spiritual Temple or the Church by the Messias; there being about a thousand years distance be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tween those two periods whereof seventy Prophetical Weeks, or four hundred and ninety years were yet to come. And so he prays that God would not root them out in this Babylonish Captivity, but would graciously restore them to their own land and preserve them as a Church and Nation there until the coming of the Messias.</ns0:note>: thy years <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> through<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out all generations <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Though we successively die and perish, yet thou art the everlasting and unchangeable God, and therefore art and wilt ever be able to deliver thy peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple, and faithful in performing all thy promises; and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore we beseech thee to pity our frail and languishing state, and give us a more setled and lasting felicity than yet we have enjoyed; and therefore we trust that thy people shall <ns0:hi>conti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nue and be established before thee,</ns0:hi> as he saith, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 28. because as thou art the everlasting God, so thou hast made an Everlast<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Covenant with them, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 105. 10. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 55. 3. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 32. 40. to be their God for ever; and therefore thou wilt not now forsake or reject us.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Heb. 1. 10.</ns0:note> Of old hast thou laid the foundation of the earth: and the heavens <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> the work of thy hands <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The Eternity of God looks both backward and forward, it is both without beginning and without end. The former is affirmed and illustrated, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 24, 26, 27. the latter is clearly implyed in this Verse, Thou hadst a being before the Crea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of the World, when there was nothing but Eternity, but the Earth and Heavens had a beginning given them by thy Al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mighty Power.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isai. 15. 6.</ns0:note> They shall perish <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Either 1. as to the substance of them, which shall be an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nihilated. Or 2. as to their present nature and use. See <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 65. 17. and 66. 22. 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3. 7, 10, 11. The Heavens and the Earth although they be the most permanent of all visible beings, and their continuance is oft mentioned to signifie the stability and immutability of things, yet if compared with thee are as nothing, they had a beginning and shall have an end.</ns0:note>, but thou shalt <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> stand.</ns0:note> en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dure: yea, all of them shall wax old <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Decay and perish.</ns0:note> like a gar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Which is worn out and laid aside, and exchanged for another. And so shall this present frame of Heaven and Earth be.</ns0:note>; as a vesture shalt thou change them, and they shall be changed.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 But thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> the same, and thy years shall have no end.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 The children of thy servants shall conti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nue <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Though the Heavens and the Earth perish, and though we thy servants <ns0:hi>pine away in our iniquities</ns0:hi> according to thy righteous sentence and threatning, <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 26. 39. and die in Captivity, yet by vertue of thy eternal and unchangeable na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture and Covenant we rest assured that our Children and their Children after them shall enjoy the promised mercies, an happy restitution to, and settlement in, their own land, and the presence of our and their Messias, whom, being not to come till after 490. years, we shall not live to see. The ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pression here used is general, not without design, partly to shew that this promised blessing belongs to the Jews not up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on the account of any carnal relation to <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> but as they are and continue to be Gods servants, from whom if they re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />volt, they lose this and all their other priviledges; and partly to imply that it belongs to all Gods faithful Servants and to their Children, whether they be Jews, or Gentiles, of whose Conversion he spoke, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 22.</ns0:note>, and their seed shall be established before thee <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">In the place of thy gracious presence, either here in thy Church, or hereafter in Heaven, from which we are now banished. And this phrase further in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />timates that their happiness did not consist in the enjoyment of the outward blessings of the land of <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> but in the pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sence and fruition of God there, which he mentions as the top and upshot of all his desires and their felicities.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

Poole.heading:
PSAL. CII. A Prayer 
                        
                           〈◊〉
                         
                        
                           〈◊〉
                        . of the afflicted when he is overwhelmed, and poureth out his complaint before the LORD This Psalm contains a form of Prayer and Expostulation with God composed for the use of all true Israelites, in the name and behalf of their Mother the Church of Israel. It seems to have been composed in the time of their Captivity and near the end of it, v. 13, 14. But as the literal Ierusalem was a type of the spiritual or of the Church of God and of Christ, and the rebuilding of the former a type of the reviving and edification of the latter, so the Psalmist looks through that mercy of the rebuilding of the City of Ierusalem and the Temple to the further progress and to the end and perfection of that work, which was in the coming of the Messiah, by whom it was to be compleated, and by whom the Gentiles were to be brought to the knowledge and worship of the true God..
